opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I've thought about a lot, partly because poker solvers are something I know really well. I spent years of my PhD building them, so I have a good sense of how hard each piece is.

The nice thing about poker as a test case is that the output is measurable. You don't have to rely on vibes. You can compute exploitability, meaning how much a perfect adversary could win against the strategy the agent produced. A solver that's close to equilibrium has very low exploitability, and a buggy or naive one is easy to beat. So you get a clean, objective signal.

Then there's the process. Building a good solver isn't one task. You need to represent the game efficiently, implement something like counterfactual regret minimization correctly, handle abstraction so the game is tractable, and manage memory and compute well. Then you need to debug it, and that's where most humans spend their time. The bugs in these systems are subtle. The strategy looks reasonable, but it's slightly wrong, and you only notice if you know which sanity checks to run.

So if I gave an agent a month, I'd want to see more than whether it produced a solver. I'd want to see whether it made progress over the month the way a strong grad student would. Does it set up its own evaluation harness? Does it notice when exploitability plateaus and figure out why? Does it try variants like CFR+ or discounting, and measure whether they help? Can it recover from going down a wrong path for a few days?

That long-horizon, self-directed research loop is the real thing being tested. Today's models are already good at writing a CFR implementation in an afternoon if you ask for one. What's much harder, and much more interesting, is sustained, coherent progress on a research problem over weeks without a human steering. If an agent could take that month and end up with something competitive with what a PhD student produces in a year or two, that would tell you a lot about where we are.

r001.rationale: The response says current models can write a CFR implementation quickly, but it does not express confidence that an agent could build a river-only poker solver.

r002.rationale: It describes sustained autonomous research progress as difficult, but does not clearly judge that an agent cannot yet build a full poker solver autonomously from a goal alone, even with a month.

r003.rationale: It offers no prediction that agents will soon produce a complete, state-of-the-art poker solver autonomously within a month.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because a poker solver is actually a really nice test case. It's a well-defined problem, we know what good looks like, and I've spent a lot of my career building these things, so I have a pretty good sense of where the hard parts are.

The first thing I'd say is that the question "can it build a poker solver" is actually several questions. Can it build something that runs? Can it build something that converges to an approximate Nash equilibrium in heads-up limit hold'em? Can it do no-limit, with the abstraction and the real-time search that made Libratus and Pluribus work? Those are wildly different levels of difficulty, and the gap between them is where I'd actually be assessing.

So concretely, if I gave an agent a month, here's what I'd look at. First, correctness, and this is the thing people underestimate. Counterfactual regret minimization is maybe a few hundred lines of code in its simplest form, but there are so many subtle ways to get it wrong where it still looks like it's working. The regrets go down, the strategy looks plausible, and it's actually converging to something that's not an equilibrium. So I'd want to see the agent build its own verification. Compute exploitability against the final strategy. Check it on Kuhn poker and Leduc, where we know the exact answers. Does it do that on its own, or does it just declare victory when the loss curve looks nice? That tells you a lot about whether it understands what it's building versus pattern-matching to what a solver looks like.

Second, I'd look at how it handles scale. The naive version of CFR doesn't work on full-size games, you have to do abstraction, you have to do sampling variants like Monte Carlo CFR, you have to think about memory layout and how you're going to store the regret tables. A month is enough time that an agent should hit those walls, and the interesting signal is what it does when it hits them. Does it recognize that it needs card abstraction, or does it just keep throwing compute at an intractable game tree? Does it discover something like discounting or linear CFR because the convergence is too slow, or does it just wait?

Third, and this is the part I'm honestly most curious about, is whether it does anything I wouldn't have thought of. When we were building these systems, the big breakthroughs were things like real-time search, depth-limited solving, the realization that you could make the game tractable by solving subgames on the fly. Those weren't obvious. They came out of years of banging our heads against the problem. If an agent working for a month rediscovers some of that, that's a big deal. If it comes up with something genuinely new, that's an even bigger deal, and I'd actually consider that the real bar.

The last thing I'd say is that a month is a really long time for an agent right now. The failure mode I'd watch for isn't that it can't write CFR, it's that it loses the thread. It gets three weeks in, has fourteen different versions of the solver, doesn't remember why it made certain decisions, and can't tell you which one is actually the best. Long-horizon coherence is the thing I think is still hard, and poker is a nice domain for exposing that because there's a very clear scoreboard at the end. You can just measure exploitability. Either it built a solver or it didn't.

r001.rationale: The response discusses several solver difficulty levels but does not mention a river-only solver or express confidence an agent could build one.

r002.rationale: It highlights challenges with scale and long-horizon coherence, but does not conclude that an agent cannot autonomously build a full solver from a goal in a month.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that agents will soon produce a complete, state-of-the-art solver autonomously; it only describes rediscovering or inventing techniques as possible assessment signals.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between building something that looks like a poker solver and building something that actually works well. If you give an agent a month, does it produce a program that runs and outputs a strategy? Or does it produce a strategy that’s difficult to exploit, and do so with reasonable compute?

Poker is nice because you can make that assessment pretty concrete. For a small game, you can measure how far the strategy is from an equilibrium. For a larger game, you can compare against existing solvers and test particular components on smaller games where you know the answer. Just having it play some hands and win isn’t enough—there’s a lot of variance, and beating a weak opponent doesn’t establish that you’ve built a good solver.

I’d also care about how much human intervention it needed over that month. Did it identify bugs, design useful experiments, and recover from approaches that didn’t work? That’s a much stronger demonstration of an agent’s ability than getting to a plausible-looking result and stopping.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating poker solvers generally but does not express confidence that a current agent could build a river-only solver.

r002.rationale: It raises whether an agent can produce a strong solver autonomously, but does not conclude that current agents are incapable of doing so from a goal alone, even with a month.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction that agents will soon autonomously produce a complete, state-of-the-art solver from a goal and a month of work.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to look at the solver it produces, rather than how long it worked or how convincing its explanation sounds. Does it actually run? How close is its strategy to equilibrium? How much compute does it need to get there?

Poker is nice because you can start with small games where you know the answer. You can check whether the agent’s implementation converges, then move to larger games and compare it against existing approaches under the same compute budget. Just playing a few matches isn’t enough, because there’s a lot of variance, and beating one opponent doesn’t establish that you’ve built a good solver.

The month-long part raises another question: can it sustain useful progress? Can it find a bug, design an experiment to isolate it, and change direction when an approach fails? I’d care much more about that than whether it can generate a plausible implementation on the first try.
